Full year results for the twelve months ended 30 June 2026

Revenue growth, new licensing agreements, and progress across therapeutic programmes

Aptamer Group plc (AIM: APTA), the developer of next-generation synthetic binders delivering innovation to the life sciences industry, today announces its full year results for the twelve months ended 30 June 2026 (the "Period").

Financial summary

Revenue £1.5 million (2025: £1.2 million), representing a 28% increase over the previous financial year. 

Cash balance at 30 June 2026: £4.4 million (2025: £1.1 million), following a £4.1 million equity raise in April 2026.

Adjusted EBITDA loss of £2.3 million (2025: £2.2 million).

Administration expenses £3.2 million (2025: £2.9 million).

The Board considers the current cash position provides runway into calendar 2028 in line with July 2026 trading update and before any further licensing receipts. 

Pipeline substantial and continues to grow as interest in technology platform widens across multiple industries.

Strategic milestone delivery

Significant commercial traction over the year, including repeat business with multiple top 20 pharmaceutical companies.

Enzyme-modulating Optimers out-licensed to Twist Bioscience and Alphazyme. Licensing terms include an upfront payment, royalties, and supply revenue, with the first licensing payments received.

Folic acid Optimers are being developed into a rapid test for food fortification as part of a programme supported by the Gates Foundation.

Second Unilever development programme was successfully completed in-house at Aptamer.

AI model architecture has been built and trained across an in-house dataset and demonstrated the ability to screen candidates, with initial Optimer® candidates currently being validated.

Fibrotic liver delivery vehicle demonstrated excellent preclinical characteristics, being non-toxic, stable, and non-immunogenic, significantly de-risking its therapeutic potential. 

Targeted radiotherapeutic programme launched with material for first in vivo animal studies delivered to partners. 

Multiple therapeutic programmes initiated with lead candidates identified for kidney targeting delivery vehicles. 

The Group has purchased and deployed new automation machinery to expand binder development and manufacturing capacity, supporting revenue growth well beyond the level required for breakeven.

Post-period developments

Increase in sales pipeline from £4.8 million at 30 June 2026 to £7.0 million at 21 September 2026. 

Following repeat orders from several top 20 pharmaceutical companies, including more than £0.5 million of spend, the Group is moving these relationships onto multi-year, multi-target master service agreements, with several in advanced negotiation. These agreements give greater revenue visibility and are central to the Group's path to EBITDA break-even. 

The Group is taking a proactive approach to developing its own licensable assets in the enzyme and cosmetics fields, building on its recent enzyme licensing success.

Cavendish Capital Markets appointed as joint corporate broker with Turner Pope Investments.

Commenting on the results, Dr Arron Tolley, Chief Executive Officer of Aptamer Group, said: 

“This has been a year of inflection for Aptamer. We have moved from proving our technology to proving our business model with two royalty-bearing licences now signed, repeat orders from multiple top 20 pharmaceutical companies, and our first entry into the radioligand therapy market. 

"Following April's fundraise, we have used the proceeds to build the foundations for the next phase of growth. Our AI programme has progressed from a standing start to candidate validation in a matter of months, our manufacturing capacity has been expanded to support partners at commercial scale, and we are now building a therapeutic pipeline spanning RNAi delivery to multiple diseases and organs including fibrosis and kidney, along with radiopharmaceuticals.

"We enter the new financial year with recurring fee-for-service demand, growing licensing income, and multiple development programmes advancing in our own pipeline. I would like to thank our partners, shareholders and the whole Aptamer team for their continued support, and I look forward to updating the market as this progress continues to build.”

About Aptamer Group plc

Aptamer Group plc (AIM: APTA) develops Optimer® binders, next-generation synthetic alternatives to antibodies that offer high specificity, improved stability, lower cost and access to targets beyond the reach of conventional modalities.

The Group operates a dual-revenue model, generating near-term revenues through fee-for-service discovery programmes while building a portfolio of proprietary therapeutic assets designed to create long-term value through licensing, royalties and supply agreements.

Aptamer is strategically focused on two of the most significant challenges in modern drug development: targeting "undruggable" proteins and enabling delivery of therapeutics to tissues beyond the liver. Its proprietary Optimer® platform, supported by more than 15 years of discovery data and an expanding AI-enabled discovery engine, is designed to accelerate the identification of high-quality binders against challenging biological targets.

The Group's internal pipeline includes targeted delivery vehicles for oligonucleotide therapeutics and radioligand therapy programmes, with upcoming in vivo studies expected to support future partnering and licensing opportunities.

Founded in 2008 and headquartered in York, UK, Aptamer works with many of the world's leading pharmaceutical companies, combining platform expertise, proprietary data and therapeutic innovation to create shareholder value.

Chairman and Chief Executive Officer’s statement

We are pleased to report a successful year for Aptamer, where we have seen continued growth, marked by initial assets being out-licensed and delivering revenue, an increase in fee-for-service revenue driven by repeat business from large pharmaceutical companies, and, following the fundraise in April 2026, investment in artificial intelligence (AI), manufacturing capacity, and initiation of our own therapeutic pipeline. 

Fee-for-service growth and returning partners

Increasing commercial engagement and high-value repeat orders from multiple top 20 pharmaceutical companies led to a 28% increase in revenue for the year compared to the previous period, to £1.5 million. After successfully testing the platform, several partners have returned with further work and larger projects, strongly endorsing the technology. 

One top 5 pharmaceutical partner awarded over £0.75 million of new contracts during the period, taking the total lifetime contract value with that customer to more than £1 million. We also secured repeat business with a top 10 and a top 20 pharmaceutical company, in both cases supporting research against targets that have proved intractable for other technologies. These repeat orders from global companies strongly validate our binder technology.

The year also brought our first commercial entry into the radioligand therapy market, through a £360,000 development contract with a top 3 global pharmaceutical company. The work involves engineering Optimer® binders as targeted radiopharmaceuticals for cancer imaging, with potential therapeutic application beyond that. Radiopharmaceuticals are now an additional therapeutic modality under active development, alongside targeted gene therapy, with targeted radiopharmaceutical requirements for precise targeting, rapid tissue penetration and clearance of unbound material, leveraging the strengths of Optimer® technology. 

Our diagnostics programme with Metir, developing Optimer® binders for the detection of Cryptosporidium in water supplies, continues to progress well. Since initiation in September 2025, the programme hit its technical feasibility milestone on time and on budget, in February 2026. The binders are now undergoing final validation at Aptamer before shipping to partners for internal testing. The global Cryptosporidium diagnostic testing market was valued at approximately US$1.2 billion in 2025 and is forecast to reach US$2.5 billion by 2033,1 highlighting the potential for Optimer® technology to support Metir’s market-first platform in this space. 

Customer asset portfolio advancement

The enzyme-modulating Optimers that were under negotiation twelve months ago are now licensed to both Twist Bioscience and Alphazyme. Each contract includes an upfront payment, ongoing royalties, and revenue from supply of the reagent itself, with first licensing payments already received. Across the two enzyme-modulating reagents now developed, four additional parties are evaluating the Optimers, with the potential for licensing depending on results. 

Our folic acid Optimers are being taken forward as a rapid test for food fortification (adding nutrients to food) under a programme supported by the Gates Foundation. The programme will investigate the suitability of Aptamer's proprietary folic acid Optimers to develop an affordable, field-deployable lateral flow test for monitoring folate levels in fortified foods in developing countries. Aptamer has contracted an upfront fee to develop sample extraction methods for this binder. These binders have subsequently been delivered to the Guder Research Group at Imperial College London for integration into lateral flow devices. 

Optimer® immunohistochemistry reagents have been successfully developed for a global life sciences conglomerate. Within the period the binders completed development, and were characterised, manufactured and delivered by Aptamer for the partner's own internal validation. Subject to that successful validation, the Optimer® will be integrated into commercial assay kits under an agreed royalty of 2% of net sales. 

The Unilever partnership continues to progress, with stability assessments successfully completed for the first Optimer® programme in the first half of the period. The second development programme for Unilever has now successfully identified binders, which have been characterised in-house at Aptamer Group. 

Increased capacity and machine learning advances

The £4.1 million of net proceeds raised in April 2026 was sought to expand manufacturing capability, fund the AI programme, develop Optimers for a range of therapeutic targets and advance Optimer® candidates through preclinical studies. 

New automation machinery was purchased during the period, which will improve the efficiency of development programmes, and add manufacturing capacity to support out-licensed assets for our partners to deliver commercial volumes for their products. We have also refined the discovery process itself, delivering a 50% increase in speed for each discovery round. Alongside this, laboratory processes for conjugation have been standardised, broadening the range of functional groups that can be added to Optimer® binders in-house, bringing work previously carried out by external partners in-house and shortening development timelines.

The artificial intelligence programme has advanced rapidly since initiation in April 2026. We have built and trained a model architecture on our discovery dataset, accumulated over years of laboratory work, and shown it can screen candidates in silico. The first Optimer® candidates produced by the model are now being validated in the laboratory ahead of an initial service launch. If validation is successful, this will enable improved customer discovery with faster timelines and support in-house development programmes. 

Building a therapeutic pipeline

During the year, the fibrotic delivery vehicle was shown to be non-toxic, stable, and non-immunogenic, providing strong evidence to support advancement to preclinical testing. Post-period, the plans to progress this molecule through in vivo animal studies for siRNA delivery have been finalised. 

In March 2026, we launched a targeted radiotherapeutic programme, in collaboration with Radiopharmium, a UK-based consultancy providing specialist expertise, contacts and access to facilities in radiopharmaceutical development, from early research to manufacturing. The first three strategic therapeutic targets to enter this programme, representing high‑value clinical conditions for which Optimer® radioconjugates will be developed, have been identified and Optimer® development started in June. The targeted radiopharmaceuticals market is valued at approximately US$5.6 billion in 2025,2 and is a high‑growth, high-priority sector, with current targeting technologies presenting well-recognised limitations. The first targeted radiotherapeutic candidate to prove the Optimer® platform has been delivered to our partners to enter animal studies. This will both prove the platform's targeting capabilities and deliver the first therapeutic Optimer® candidate for potential out-licensing to partners. 

We have also started several further therapeutic discovery programmes. We identified lead candidates for kidney-targeting delivery vehicles, and work on brain targeting began during the period. Since year end, additional targets have entered discovery across both targeted delivery and the selected panel of difficult-to-drug biomarkers identified by the Group. 

Post-period momentum

Since year end, we have begun implementing a commercial strategy to convert repeat business into longer-term, higher-volume partnerships. Multiple top 20 pharmaceutical companies have each spent more than £500,000 with the Group, and we are now working with several of them to put in place multi-year, multi-target master service agreements. Reflecting this, the sales pipeline has expanded to £7.0 million at 21 September 2026, driven primarily by a number of large contracts under negotiation with pharmaceutical partners. 

These agreements pre-agree commercial terms so that partners can commission work quickly and at scale, without renegotiating project by project. By shortening the path from a partner's decision to project start, we expect them to increase repeat ordering and build a more consistent order book, giving us good visibility of revenue growth and supporting our path to EBITDA break-even. Given the scale and complexity of these contracts, additional time is required to finalise terms and put the operational framework in place with each partner. The benefit of these longer-term agreements will build as each is signed, replacing one-off project orders with recurring demand that improves revenue visibility, allows capacity planning, and spreads the Group's fixed cost base over higher volumes.

Technical delivery has seen the folic acid Optimers delivered to the Guder Research Group at Imperial College London for integration into lateral flow devices, following successful completion of field-compatible sample preparation with Optimer® shown to perform in multiple different foodstuffs, and plans finalised to progress the fibrotic liver delivery vehicle into in vivo animal studies. Additional targets have also entered discovery across both targeted delivery and our selected panel of difficult-to-drug biomarkers, further broadening the base from which future licensing opportunities can be drawn. In parallel, we have begun proactively developing our own licensable assets in the enzyme and cosmetics fields. 

Outlook

With two royalty-bearing licensing agreements now signed and further parties in discussion, a sales pipeline that has expanded to £7.0 million, and a therapeutic pipeline spanning fibrotic disease, kidney and brain delivery, and radiopharmaceuticals now underway, Aptamer enters the new financial year with a materially different business than it had twelve months ago. Fee-for-service and repeating demand from the world's largest pharmaceutical companies continues to broaden, our capacity to meet that demand has been expanded through new automation, and a therapeutic pipeline spanning fibrotic disease, kidney and brain delivery, and radiopharmaceuticals is now underway.

The AI programme adds a further dimension to this growth. As the model moves from validation into service, we expect it to shorten discovery timelines for our partners in the near term and support the design of entirely new Optimer® sequences in the longer term, improving the platform’s speed and economics and broadening its target potential.

With a strengthened balance sheet, an increasingly diversified asset portfolio, and deepening relationships across pharmaceutical, diagnostic and consumer partners, the Board is confident in the Group's ability to convert this progress into added value to shareholders. We look forward to another year of growth as interest in the Optimer® platform continues to gather pace. The prospects for Aptamer in 2027 and beyond remain very encouraging.

 1 Accounting policies

Company information

Aptamer Group Plc (“the Company”) is a company limited by shares, domiciled, and incorporated in the United Kingdom and registered in England and Wales. The registered office is Windmill House, Innovation Way, York, YO10 5BR. 

The Group consists of Aptamer Group Plc and all of its subsidiaries. The Group is a leading provider of Optimer® reagents for use by customers in research, diagnostics and therapeutics. The Group has developed a platform technology which is utilised to solve problems for pharmaceutical and bio-technology customers in the bioprocessing, research reagents, diagnostic and therapeutic areas of the life sciences.

1.1 Basis of preparation

The financial information included in this annual results announcement for the year ended 30 June 2026 does not constitute the Group's statutory accounts. Statutory accounts for the period ended 30 June 2025 have been delivered to the Registrar of Companies. The statutory accounts for the year ended 30 June 2026 were approved by the Board on 12 October 2026 and will be delivered to the Registrar of Companies in due course. The Auditor's report on those accounts for the year ended 30 June 2026 was unqualified, made reference to material uncertainty with regard to the going concern basis, and did not contain a statement under 498(2) or 498(3).

These Group financial statements have been prepared in accordance with UK-adopted International Financial Reporting Standards (“IFRS”) and IFRS Interpretations Committee (“IFRIC”) Interpretations that are applicable to the consolidated financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2026, in conformity with the requirements of the Companies Act 2006.

These financial statements are prepared in sterling which is the functional currency of the Group and the Company. Monetary amounts in these financial statements are rounded to the nearest £’000.

The financial statements have been prepared under the historical cost convention, modified to include certain financial instruments at fair value.

The principal accounting policies adopted are set out below. The accounting policies have been consistently applied to all the periods presented, unless otherwise stated.

1.2 Basis of consolidation

The consolidated financial statements incorporate those of Aptamer Group Plc and all of its subsidiaries (i.e. entities where the Group is exposed, or has rights, to variable returns from its involvement and has the ability to affect those returns through its power). The subsidiaries consolidated in these Group accounts were acquired via Group reorganisation and as such merger accounting principles have been applied. The financial statements of the Company and its subsidiaries are made up to 30 June 2026.

All intra-group transactions, balances and unrealised gains on transactions between Group companies are eliminated on consolidation. Unrealised losses are also eliminated unless the transaction provides evidence of an impairment of the asset transferred.

1.3 Going concern

The Group has reported a loss after tax for the year ended 30 June 2026 of £1.86 million (year ended 30 June 2025: £2.4 million). The Group had a cash balance of £4.4 million at 30 June 2026 (30 June 2025: £1.1 million) following the completion of a fundraise in April 2026, which raised proceeds of £4.1 million after expenses.

The Directors have considered the applicability of the going concern basis in the preparation of these financial statements, which includes assessing an internal forecast extending out to June 2028. The Directors consider that this forecast represents a reasonable best estimate of the performance of the Group over the period to June 2028. 

During the year to 30 June 2026 the Group has reported revenues of £1.5 million which is up from £1.2 million in the prior year. Additionally, the Group has licensed its first two assets during the year, which have started generating recurring licensing revenue. The Company has a number of further assets which have the potential to add licensing revenue to the Group as they each approach commercialisation. 

Management continue to maintain close control of costs to maximise the cash runway.

In the forecast, full year revenue for the year to 30 June 2027 is anticipated to be higher than was the case in the year to June 2026. Within this forecast, delivery of these expectations would ensure that the resultant positive cashflows together with the current cash balance are sufficient to see the Group into calendar year 2028.

The Directors have also considered reasonably likely downside scenarios, which includes slower growth in core revenues.

Should these downside scenarios materialise, the Group may need to seek additional funding. The Directors have a reasonable expectation that the Group could access further funding, from both dilutive and non-dilutive sources. However, there can be no guarantee that the Group would be able to raise additional funding from an equity fundraise to new and existing investors, nor that the Group will successfully develop further assets for licensing within the period to 2028.

Based on the above factors the Directors believe that it remains appropriate to prepare Group and Company financial statements on a going concern basis. 1.4 Revenue from contracts with customers

Research activities 

The Group’s main source of revenue is fees for research activities carried out under contracts with customers. These contracts can be in progress over accounting period ends and consist of separate phases with fixed attributable income attached to each phase. The contract contains performance obligations set out for each phase. In most cases that customer has a right to proceed or cease the research work at the end of each phase.

The Group recognises revenue when it satisfies the performance obligations in respect of each phase of work. As a result, revenue is recognised over time as each performance obligation is satisfied, by reference to the work performed in delivering the performance obligations to the customer. Where consideration is received in advance of the performance obligations being fulfilled, a contract liability is recognised; where performance obligations are fulfilled in advance of an invoice being delivered to the customer, a contract asset is recognised.

No revenue is recognised in relation to subsequent contract phases until the customer has elected to progress to that phase and the above criteria in relation to satisfaction of performance obligations has been met. 

Costs incurred in fulfilling a contract phase, which include internal labour costs and materials, are recognised in the balance sheet until the satisfaction of performance obligations where: 

the costs relate directly to a contract that the Group can specifically identify; 

the costs generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying (or in continuing to satisfy) performance obligations in the future; and 

the costs are expected to be recovered.

Following performance obligations being satisfied, the revenue is recognised by reference to the contractual value of that performance obligation and amounts capitalised in-line with the above are recognised as an expense on a basis consistent with the recognition of the related revenue.

Licensing

Supply of Products

The Group supplies products under a fixed price for each product supplied. Revenue is recognised at the point in time at which control is transferred. This is taken to be on dispatch of each unit.

Licence fee income

The Group also enters into licensing arrangements with its customers, wherein they are granted rights to access the group’s intellectual property. Revenue attributable to the licence is recognised over the licence period. Revenue is recognised over discrete periods of licensing based on the unit quantities used by the customer which incorporates the relevant intellectual property. 

Income from royalties

Certain licensing arrangements entitle the Group to royalties calculated as a percentage of the customer’s onward sales of products incorporating the Group’s intellectual property. Sales-based royalties arising from licensing intellectual property are recognised when the subsequent sale by the customer has been reported to the Group.

1.5 Research and development expenditure

An intangible asset arising from development (or from the development phase of an internal project) is recognised where the following criteria are met: 

it is technically feasible to complete the intangible asset so that it will be available for use or sale; 

management intends to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it; 

there is ability to use or sell the intangible asset; 

it can be demonstrated that the intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits; 

there is evidence of existence of a market for the output of the intangible asset or the intangible asset itself or, if it is to be used internally, the usefulness of the intangible asset; 

adequate technical, financial and other resources exist to complete the development and to use or sell the intangible asset; and 

the expenditure attributable to the intangible asset during its development can be reliably measured. 

Research expenditure and development expenditure that do not meet the criteria above are written off against results in the year in which they are incurred. Identifiable development expenditure is capitalised to the extent that the technical, commercial and financial feasibility can be demonstrated.

1.9 Impairment of tangible and intangible assets

At each reporting end date, the Group reviews the carrying amounts of its tangible and intangible assets on an individual and on a cash-generating unit basis to determine whether there is any indication that those assets have suffered an impairment loss. If any such indication exists, the recoverable amount of the asset is estimated in order to determine the extent of the impairment loss (if any). Where it is not possible to estimate the recoverable amount of an individual asset, the Group estimates the recoverable amount of the cash-generating unit to which the asset belongs.

Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell, and value in use. In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time-value of money and the risks specific to the asset for which the estimates of future cash flows have not been adjusted.

If the recoverable amount of an asset (or cash-generating unit) is estimated to be less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset (or cash-generating unit) is reduced to its recoverable amount. An impairment loss is recognised immediately in the Consolidated Statement of Comprehensive Income, unless the relevant asset is carried at a revalued amount in which case the impairment loss is treated as a revaluation decrease.

Recognised impairment losses are reversed if, and only if, the reasons for the impairment loss have ceased to apply. Where an impairment loss subsequently reverses, the carrying amount of the asset (or cash-generating unit) is increased to the revised estimate of its recoverable amount, but so that the increased carrying amount does not exceed the carrying amount that would have been determined had no impairment loss been recognised for the asset (or cash-generating unit) in prior years. A reversal of an impairment loss is recognised immediately in the income statement, unless the relevant asset is carried at a revalued amount, in which case the reversal of the impairment loss is treated as a revaluation increase.

Financial instruments are recognised in the Group's statement of financial position when the Group becomes party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. 

Financial assets and liabilities are offset, and the net amounts presented in the financial statements, when there is a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net basis or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously.

Financial assets are recognised in the Group’s statement of financial position when the Group becomes party to the contractual provisions of the instrument. Financial assets are classified into specified categories, depending on the nature and purpose of the financial assets. 

The Group classifies its financial assets in the following measurement categories:

those to be measured subsequently at fair value (either through Other comprehensive income (OCI) or through profit or loss); and 

those to be measured at amortised cost.

They arise principally from the provision of goods and services to customers (e.g. trade receivables). They are initially recognised at fair value plus transaction costs directly attributable to their acquisition or issue, and are subsequently carried at amortised cost using the effective interest rate method, less provision for impairment where necessary.

Debt instruments 

Subsequent measurement of debt instruments depends on the Group’s business model for managing the asset and the cash flow characteristics of the asset. There are three measurement categories into which the Group classifies its debt instruments: 

Amortised cost: Assets that are held for collection of contractual cash flows, where those cash flows represent solely payments of principal and interest, are measured at amortised cost. Interest income from these financial assets is included in finance income using the effective interest rate method. The Group recognises loss allowances for expected credit losses on financial assets measured at amortised cost. Derecognition of financial assets

1.15 Taxation

The income tax expense or credit represents the sum of the tax currently payable or receivable on the current period’s taxable income or loss, based on the applicable income tax rate for each jurisdiction, adjusted by changes in deferred tax assets and liabilities attributable to temporary differences and to unused tax losses.

Current tax

The tax currently payable or receivable is based on taxable profit or loss for the period. Taxable profit differs from net profit as reported in the profit and loss account because it excludes items of income or expense that are taxable or deductible in other years and it further excludes items that are never taxable or deductible. 

The Group’s liability for current tax is calculated using tax rates that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the reporting end date. Management periodically evaluates positions taken in tax returns with respect to situations in which applicable tax regulation is subject to interpretation. It establishes provisions, where appropriate, on the basis of amounts expected to be paid to the tax authorities. 

Current tax assets and tax liabilities are offset where the entity has a legally enforceable right to offset and intends either to settle on a net basis, or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. 

Deferred tax

Deferred income tax is provided in full, using the liability method, on temporary differences arising between the tax bases of assets and liabilities and their carrying amounts in the consolidated financial statements. However, deferred tax liabilities are not recognised if they arise from the initial recognition of goodwill. Deferred income tax is also not accounted for if it arises from initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction other than a business combination that, at the time of the transaction, affects neither accounting nor taxable profit or loss. Deferred income tax is determined using tax rates (and laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period and are expected to apply when the related deferred income tax asset is realised or the deferred income tax liability is settled. 

Deferred tax assets are recognised only if it is probable that future taxable amounts will be available to utilise those temporary differences and losses. 

Deferred tax liabilities and assets are not recognised for temporary differences between the carrying amount and tax bases of investments in foreign operations where the Company is able to control the timing of the reversal of the temporary differences and it is probable that the differences will not reverse in the foreseeable future. 

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset where there is a legally enforceable right to offset current tax assets and liabilities and where the deferred tax balances relate to the same taxation authority. 

1.16 Provisions

Provisions for legal claims and make good obligations are recognised when the Group has a legal or constructive present obligation as a result of a past event, it is probable that the Group will be required to settle that obligation and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. Provisions are not recognised for future operating losses.

Where there are a number of similar obligations, the likelihood that an outflow will be required in settlement is determined by considering the class of obligations as a whole. A provision is recognised even if the likelihood of an outflow with respect to any one item included in the same class of obligations may be small.

The amount recognised as a provision is the management’s best estimate of the consideration required to settle the present obligation at the reporting end date, taking into account the risks and uncertainties surrounding the obligation. The discount rate used to determine the present value is a pre-tax rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability. The increase in the provision due to the passage of time is recognised as interest expense.

1.18 Leases

On commencement of a contract which gives the Group the right to use an asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration, the Group recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability unless the lease qualifies as a ‘short-term’ lease (term is 12 months or less with no option to purchase the lease asset) or a ‘low-value’ lease (where the underlying asset is £4,000 or less when new).

Initial measurement of the lease liability

The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments during the lease term, discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease, or the incremental borrowing rate if the interest rate implicit in the lease cannot be readily determined.

To determine the incremental borrowing rate, the Group: 

where possible, uses recent third-party financing received by the individual lessee as a starting point, adjusted to reflect changes in financing conditions since third-party financing was received; 

uses a build-up approach that starts with a risk-free interest rate adjusted for credit risk for leases held by the Group, which does not have recent third-party financing; and 

makes adjustments specific to the lease, e.g. term, country, currency and security.

The lease is the non-cancellable period of the lease plus extension periods that the Group is reasonably certain to exercise and termination periods that the Group is reasonably certain not to exercise. 

Lease payments include fixed payments, less any lease incentives receivable, variable lease payments dependent on an index or a rate, amounts expected to be payable by the Group under residual value guarantees and payments of penalties for terminating the lease, if the lease term reflects the Group exercising that option. Variable lease payments are initially measured using the index or rate when the leased asset is available for use. The cost of the right-of-use asset also includes any provisions expected to be settled on termination of the lease.

Subsequent measurement of the lease liability

The lease liability is subsequently increased for a constant periodic rate of interest on the remaining balance of the lease liability and reduced for lease payments.

Interest on the lease liability is recognised in the income statement. Variable lease payments not included in the measurement of the lease liability as they are not dependent on an index or rate are recognised in the income statement in the period in which the event or condition that triggers those payments occurs.

When the lease liability is remeasured due to changes arising from the original terms and conditions of the lease, the corresponding adjustment is reflected in the right-of-use asset, or income statement if the right-of-use asset is already reduced to nil.

A lease modification that was not part of the original terms and conditions of the lease is accounted for as a separate lease or an adjustment to the lease liability depending on the nature of the change.

A grant that specifies performance conditions is recognised in income when the performance conditions are met. Research and development expenditure credits

Functional and presentation currency

Items included in the financial statements of each of the Group’s entities are measured using the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates (‘the functional currency”). The consolidated financial statements are presented in Great British Pounds sterling, which is the functional and presentation currency of each of the Group’s entities.

Transactions and balances 

Transactions in currencies other than functional currency are recorded at the rates of exchange prevailing at the dates of the transactions. At each reporting end date, monetary +assets and liabilities that are denominated in foreign currencies are retranslated at the rates prevailing on the reporting end date. Non-monetary items that are measured at fair value in a foreign currency are translated using the exchange rates at the date when the fair value was determined. Translation differences on assets and liabilities carried at fair value are reported as part of the fair value gain or loss. 3 Judgements and key sources of estimation uncertainty

In the application of the Group’s accounting policies, the Directors are required to make judgements, estimates and assumptions about the carrying amount of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources. The estimates and associated assumptions are based on historical experience and other factors that are considered to be relevant. Actual results may differ from these estimates.

The estimates, judgements, and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to accounting estimates are recognised in the period in which the estimate is revised, if the revision affects only that period, or in the period of the revision and future periods if the revision affects both current and future periods.

Estimates and judgements are continually evaluated and are based on historical experience and other factors, including expectations of future events that are believed to be reasonable under the circumstances.

The estimates and judgements that have a significant risk of causing a material adjustment to the carrying amount of assets and liabilities within the next financial year are addressed below.

(i) Recognition of revenue from multiple element contracts, and revenue recognition

Management uses judgement in determining the fair value of multiple elements in a contract in order to appropriately recognise the revenue attributable to each element, which may be based on contractual terms, the number of days in each project phase, or (for bundled contracts) the standalone selling price that would be attributed to each service. 

For revenues recognised over time, the value of revenue recognised in the period is dependent on an assessment of work to completion. For revenues received in relation to the licensing of its intellectual property, the Group recognises this income on a straight-line basis over the licensing period. The arrangement constitutes a right to access the intellectual property and, as such, revenue attributable to these licences is therefore recognised on a straight-line basis over the licensing period, as management considers this to reflect the manner in which the Group satisfies the related performance obligation.

Where certain licensing arrangements entitle the Group to sales-based royalties, royalty revenue is recognised, in accordance with IFRS 15, when the later of the following occurs: the underlying onward sale or the satisfaction, or partial satisfaction, of the related performance obligation. Royalty revenue is calculated using sales information reported to the Group by the licensee. Any fixed fees receivable under these arrangements are recognised upon the initial grant of the licence where the related performance obligation is satisfied at that point.

(ii) Impairment of trade and other receivables 

The Group makes an estimate of the recoverable value of trade and other receivables. When assessing impairment of trade and other debtors, management considers factors including the credit rating of the receivable, the ageing profile of receivables and historical experience. As at 30 June 2026 the provision for receivables impairment amounted to £24,000 (2025: £35,000).

(iii) Impairment of investments and recoverability of intercompany loans (Company only)

Interests in subsidiary undertakings are reviewed annually to assess whether there is objective evidence to indicate that either the carrying value of interests are impaired or impairments recognised in prior periods require to be reversed. The recoverable amount of the net investment in the subsidiary undertaking is estimated as the higher of value-in-use or fair value less cost of disposal. Fair value is based on net assets and incorporates adjustments to reflect the fair market value. See note 19 for the carrying amount of the investments.

Management further utilises judgement when assessing the recoverability of intercompany loans using the expected credit loss method in accordance with the requirements of IFRS 9 ‘Financial Instruments’. Based on these forecasts, all amounts due from subsidiaries have been fully provided for at 30 June 2026.

(iv) Impairment of non-monetary assets

Product development and registration costs are recognised at historical cost and are amortised on a straight-line basis over their useful life, which is typically up to 15 years. In the case of registration costs where the asset is not in use, amortisation commences from the date of grant.

The Group assesses these assets, and all other non-monetary assets including property, plant and equipment and right-of-use assets, for impairment on an annual basis by comparing the carrying value of the single cash-generating unit (“CGU”) with the recoverable amount, the recoverable amount being based on an assessment of the CGU’s value-in-use. The Group uses discounted cashflows from the CGU to determine the value-in-use. The Group sensitises these results and determines if there is an impairment of the non-monetary assets. Further details are provided in notes 5 and 16.

(v) Share-based payments

Valuation of share-based payments requires assumptions about the achievement of non-market conditions including staff retention and target achievement and the number of options that will vest. If actual performance is different from these assumptions, costs recorded in future periods will be different from expectations and will include revisions to amounts recognised so far. Details of the key inputs and assumptions are provided in note 33.

(vi) Sublet assets

The Group and Company sublet part of a right-of-use asset during a previous year on an operating lease. The portion let is not separable from the right-of-use asset and therefore the Group has continued to classify this as a right-of-use asset at cost less depreciation, despite the sublet portion otherwise meeting the definition of an investment property.

Approach and outcome of impairment testing 

The Directors prepare forecasts which show the projected growth of the business and use of these assets, which forms a key part of the Group’s future strategy. The forecasts include an assessment of the likely commercialisation of the technology based on current demand and anticipated market growth strategies, profiled on a discounted cash flow basis which is further probability weighted for certain sensitivities around key forecasts and the timing of these. This approach is consistent with the review performed in the previous year. 

An impairment review at 30 June 2026 identified no impairment. The forecast revenues are risk-adjusted for the potential service use of each asset, as an addition to the overall revenues and costs associated with the Group’s current fee-for-service revenues. This showed that the cashflow forecasts on a risk cautious basis carried a present value in excess of the carrying value of the CGU (and were also substantially aligned with the previous year when the forecast cashflows also carried a present value in excess of the carrying value of the CGU). As a result, the Directors are confident that there is no impairment in the carrying value of the CGU this year.

The outcome of the impairment model in both the current and prior years implies that there is a reversal of the impairment of the CGU recorded in 2023’s financial statements. However, the forecast model is highly sensitive to judgemental risks associated with each asset, and in the view of the Directors no individual asset has substantial certainty around its use and commercialisation, although in the current year certain commercialisation contracts have commenced at a low value level which justifies the view of the Directors as to the commercial viability of the projects. Despite this, there is primarily anticipatory evidence only that the service potential of the assets in the CGU has improved. Because of this, and the sensitive variables in the risk-adjusted cashflow model, the Directors do not believe that there is sufficient evidence to reliably reverse the previous impairment recognised with any level of requisite precision. However, despite this uncertainty the Directors remain optimistic that the discounted cashflows of the CGU remain in excess of the carrying value of the assets at the year end.

Key inputs to discounted cashflow model

The forecasts used were for a specific period of 5 years, with revenue and costs subsequently growing at 2% per annum. In the current year the forecasts have focussed on certain key customer projects being converted, and the timing of these, which covered the estimated life of each project (up to 13 years). No terminal value was considered after termination of these projects. Costs were inflated to reflect expected adjustments over the 13 year period.

The key unobservable input to the model was:

A pre-tax discount rate of 31.99% (2025 – 31.52%), equating to a post-tax discount rate of 26.20% (2025 - 25.40%).

The main forecasts assumed the going concern status of the Group as arising from the most recent fundraise round in March and April 2026, and its planned use of funds. 

The forecast for 2026 also reflected the risk to the timing and included a probability weighting of 60% for the original forecast and 40% for an alternative in which all income from projects occurs one year later. If this alternative happens the value in use of the CGU will be reduced to £210,000.

Cashflow projections have been produced for a 13 year period because this is a prudent estimate of the expected product life cycle. No terminal values or perpetuity growth factors have been considered.

Sensitivities in the impairment model

The Directors considered sensitivities to revenue and discount rate in the cashflow forecast and the weighting applied between successful and unsuccessful fundraise post period end. If forecasted revenue in the cashflow forecast was reduced by more than 14.29% (2025 – 42.24%), this would result in a further impairment charge of £643,000 (2025 - £638,000), which would reduce the value in use of the CGU to £nil. If the post-tax discount rate was increased by 10.74% (2025 – 18.24%) then this would result in an additional impairment of £643,000 (2025 - £638,000).

The model is also sensitive to changes in individual assets’ risk reduction rates, for potential future cashflows. Disclosure of the rates used for individual assets is commercially sensitive and accordingly no sensitivity disclosure is provided.

The Directors are confident that the value of the CGU as at the date of approval of the financial statements is in excess of the carrying value as at 30 June 2026.

Further, the Directors are confident that the carrying value of the CGU has the potential to be in excess of that recognised as probabilities used for each project are considered cautious. If any uncertainties around the timing and completion of projects are closed positively then the forecasts present an outcome in excess of the carrying value of the CGU.

In the prior year, additional share options were granted (“the Award”) to rebase the options to reflect dilution caused by significant fundraises. These are equity-settled share-based payments and were valued by an independent valuation specialist using a Monte Carlo simulation, incorporating the share-price conditions necessary to achieve a payoff.

The Award was granted on 6 December 2024. The valuation inputs included a period of up to ten years within which the share-price targets could be achieved, volatility of 88.87%, a dividend yield of 0%, a risk-free rate of 4.276% and an exercise price of £0.002 per share. These historical valuation inputs continue to form the basis of the charge for the Award.

Equivalent inputs were used in the Monte Carlo simulation for the 2023 scheme, which was substantially modified as part of the grant of the 2024 scheme options. The incremental fair value arising from the modification was £1,081,035, measured by reference to the original and modified awards at the modification date. The charge for the arrangements comprises the remaining unrecognised grant-date fair value of the 2023 Award together with the incremental fair value of the modification, recognised over the applicable remaining vesting periods.

Volatility was a significant input to the valuation model. The assumption used was based on the observed volatility of the Group’s share price on the Alternative Investment Market from flotation to the grant date. At the valuation date, the Group’s recent challenges and changes, together with its continuing growth and product commercialisation, supported the expectation that similar volatility could be experienced in the short to medium term. Benchmarking against similar quoted companies indicated volatility of approximately 60%; using that assumption would have reduced the historical fair value of the Award by approximately £370,000.

The options have an exercise price of 0.2p, equal to the price at which the Company’s fundraise was completed in July and August 2024. One third of the options vest once the share price has remained at or above seven times the issue price for at least three months and become exercisable six months after vesting. A further third vest once the share price has remained at or above ten times the issue price for at least three months and become exercisable twelve months after vesting. The final third vest once the share price has remained at or above 12.5 times the issue price for at least three months and become exercisable twenty-four months after vesting.

All in-the-money share options vest if the Company is acquired. This includes a person, group or entity acquiring, or entering into a definitive binding agreement to acquire, more than 50% of the Company’s issued share capital, or assets of the Company or its subsidiaries representing more than 50% of the consolidated earning power of the Company and its subsidiaries taken as a whole.

Before the modification, the expense for the 2023 Award reflected the Directors’ assessment of the likelihood of achieving the revenue conditions for FY2025 and FY2026, together with estimated participant retention. The modification removed those non-market revenue performance conditions from the 2024 Award. The remaining share-price hurdles were incorporated into the fair value of the Award.

During the current year, the Group continued to recognise share-based payment expense in respect of these arrangements and accounted for forfeitures. Where options are forfeited because an applicable service or other non-market vesting condition is not satisfied, the related cumulative expense is adjusted accordingly. Expense is not reversed solely because a share-price hurdle is not achieved where all other vesting conditions have been satisfied, or because vested options subsequently lapse.

The total expense recognised in the income statement from equity-settled share-based payments during the year, including the effect of forfeitures, is disclosed in note 6.
